title: Apoptosis and Oncogenes
terms: Depends on two things, like birth vs death rate: cells going through the cell cycle vs cells dying.
Programmed cell death; most common form (~12 types now described). Controlled, signaled; DNA fragmented, contents not spilled.
Cells told to die (vs cells dying unbidden); apoptosis principles apply to most of its ~12 types.
Membrane-wrapped bubbles of cytoplasm the apoptotic cell packages itself into, after DNA is catalytically fragmented.
★ Contents wrapped in membrane, not spilled into the extracellular matrix (ECM) → immune system not triggered: "non-inflammatory form of cell death."
Normal apoptosis shaping the body: digit formation (absent → webbed or joined fingers) and neuron pruning (brain/spinal circuits).
Normal apoptosis removing damaged or diseased cells.
Normal apoptosis retiring cells, e.g. liver cells that get damaged detoxifying are replaced every few months.
Normal apoptosis removing immune cells after a response, e.g. excess CD8+ (cluster of differentiation 8) T cells.
★ Uncontrolled death from acute/severe stress; cell ruptures, cytoplasm leaks → damage signals → inflammation.
Released intracellular contents from ruptured cells that signal "something is wrong" → immune activation, inflammation.
Mitosis and apoptosis balanced; tissue cell number stable.
Mitosis ↑ and/or apoptosis ↓: more cells than the tissue needs (pathology term), e.g. cancers.
Mitosis ↓ and/or apoptosis ↑, when pathological = degenerative disease, e.g. neuron loss in Parkinson's.
Cell fate (embryology), removal of trophic/growth factors, DNA damage, immune death signals, extreme Ca2+ release → all converge on caspases.
Intracellular proteases made as inactive procaspases (zymogens); once activated, cut up DNA and package the cell.
Inactive enzyme precursor that must be activated (here: procaspase → caspase).
★ Caspase 8 or 9 — two initiators = two pathways (9 = internal, 8 = external); activate the effectors.
Caspase 3, 6, 7; take apart the nucleus and cell, package it for removal.
★ Cell monitors itself ("is everything okay?"): Bax vs Bcl-2 → cytochrome C → caspase 9.
★ Outside signal (immune system: "you have become dangerous"): FasL → Fas → FADD → caspase 8.
★ "Bax is bad": in the mitochondrial membrane, OPENS pores → cytochrome C escapes → death. ↑ by p53 (DNA damage).
★ Opposite of Bax ("live"): in the mitochondrial membrane, CLOSES pores. ↑ by growth/trophic factors (and AKT).
Normally in the mitochondrial intermembrane space carrying electrons complex III → IV; in the cytoplasm = "something is really wrong."
Binds released cytochrome C to build the apoptosome. Expansion not given (OUTSIDE: apoptotic protease activating factor 1 — confirm).
Large cytochrome C + Apaf-1 complex; cleaves procaspase 9 → caspase 9.
Internal-pathway initiator; procaspase 9 cleaved by the apoptosome → caspase 9 → caspases 3, 6, 7.
Growth/survival signals that ↑ Bcl-2; their REMOVAL ("I must not be needed") triggers apoptosis.
Damage sensing (DNA damage → p53 → ↑ Bax), removal of trophic factors; figure also: oxidative stress + Ca2+ overload.
★ Constant tug of war; the RATIO decides how close the cell is to apoptosis. Many signals integrate here.
↑ Bcl-2/↓ Bax → tissue grows (proliferation); balanced → homeostasis; ↑ Bax/↓ Bcl-2 → regression/degeneration. Not always pathological.
Not the internal-pathway trigger — it crosses membranes anyway; CYTOCHROME C release is what triggers it.
Death receptor expressed by almost all cells; FasL binding → Fas HOMOtrimerizes → binds FADD.
Agonist for Fas; expressed by cytotoxic T cells (and some tumors).
Fas-associated death domain; recruited by trimerized Fas; activates procaspase 8.
★ Any protein ending in DD (FADD, TRADD) probably triggers an apoptotic pathway.
TNF-alpha (tumor necrosis factor alpha) receptor-associated death domain; another DD protein.
External initiator; FADD → caspase 8, which cleaves MORE procaspase 8 (self-amplifying loop) → 3, 6, 7.
Cytotoxic CD8+ T cell recognizes a bad cell (via MHC I, major histocompatibility complex class I), expresses FasL → target dies. One of several weapons.
★ Newly activated CD8+ T cells DON'T express Fas → expand freely; as they mature they express Fas → kill each other → contraction.
Tumor gains a mutation to express FasL → triggers Fas on CD8+ T cells → kills them faster than they kill it.
★ Mutated or overexpressed gene that can cause cancer (the already-mutated form).
★ Normal gene (signaling, cell cycle, apoptosis) that becomes an oncogene when it GAINS activity (mutated, misregulated, overexpressed).
★ Gene (damage surveillance, negative cell cycle regulation) that causes cancer when it LOSES activity.
★ "Look at these pathways and decide": gain of activity → cancer = proto-oncogene; loss of activity → cancer = tumor suppressor.
Proto-oncogene, monomeric GTPase; its GTPase activity is the natural off switch. Mutated Ras can't hydrolyze GTP → always on.
Mitogen-activated protein kinase cascade downstream of Ras; activates Myc/Jun/Fos → G1/S.
Transcription factors made constantly by mutated Ras signaling; push the cell repeatedly into the cell cycle.
Proto-oncogene; normally on only when PDPK1 activates it; ↑ Bcl-2. Mutated AKT always on → ↑ Bcl-2 → blocks apoptosis.
Upstream of AKT: phosphoinositide 3-kinase makes PIP3; PDPK1 (PIP3-dependent protein kinase 1) activates AKT (LC31).
★ Tumor suppressor; critical control component. Normally stops the cycle (p21) AND potentiates apoptosis (↑ Bax). Mutated = can't be activated.
DNA damage-sensing kinase that phosphorylates (activates) p53.
Made by active p53; inhibits cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) so the damaged cell can't advance.
Retinoblastoma protein; binds and inactivates E2F. CDK phosphorylates Rb → E2F released.
Transcription factor for DNA replication genes; free E2F goes to nucleus and drives the cell cycle.
Tumor suppressor; a kinase only when bound to Axin/GSK3 → phosphorylates beta-catenin. Mutated APC can't bind → no kinase.
Partners APC must bind to act as a kinase on beta-catenin. OUTSIDE (confirm): GSK3 = glycogen synthase kinase 3.
Never phosphorylated when APC is mutated → always to nucleus → way too much cyclin D.
Wnt signaling stabilizes beta-catenin; beta-catenin acts with LEF/TCF transcription factors (figure labels).
Cell cycle regulator transcribed by beta-catenin; constant production pushes the cell through the cycle.
Oncogene delivered by a virus that causes tumorigenesis (NOT TESTED — Basel cut the Viral Oncogenes objective).
Viral Ras: constitutively active, cannot hydrolyze GTP (NOT TESTED — Basel cut the Viral Oncogenes objective).
Carries viral oncogenes E6 and E7; cause of cervical and other cancers (NOT TESTED — Basel cut the Viral Oncogenes objective).
HPV protein → ubiquitination and degradation of p53 (NOT TESTED — Basel cut the Viral Oncogenes objective).
HPV protein that binds Rb so it cannot inhibit E2F (NOT TESTED — Basel cut the Viral Oncogenes objective).
9-year-old dog: weight loss, diarrhea, anorexia, nodular colon masses, high mitotic index. Basel: "she has colon cancer ... that's easy."
Variation in cell size / nucleus size; biopsy signs of neoplasia in the case.
Normal epithelium → APC → Ras (adenoma) → p53 (carcinoma) → metastasis. Slides only; not walked through — likely low priority.
Because cell cycle regulation is redundant, cancers rarely come from a single mutation (slides only).
traps: ★ "Bax is bad": Bax OPENS mitochondrial pores (death); Bcl-2 CLOSES them (live). Don't flip them. (S10, transcript)
Initiator = 8 or 9; effector = 3, 6, 7. Initiator activates effector, never the reverse. (S8)
Cytochrome C + Apaf-1 = apoptosome → procaspase 9, not 8. The trigger is cytochrome C release, not superoxide. (S10, transcript)
p53 ↑ Bax (DNA damage → death); growth/trophic factors ↑ Bcl-2 (survival). AKT also ↑ Bcl-2. (S10, S20, transcript)
★ Apoptosis = NON-inflammatory (membrane blebs, contents not spilled); necrosis = inflammatory (rupture → DAMPs). (S5–S6, transcript)
Fas HOMOtrimerizes (Basel corrected himself from "hetero"). Caspase 8 cleaves more procaspase 8 = self-amplifying loop. (transcript)
★ T-cell homeostasis: new CD8+ T cells lack Fas (expand); mature ones express Fas (kill each other). Tumor anti-immunity: the tumor expresses FasL. (S14, transcript)
★ Proto-oncogene → cancer when it GAINS activity (Ras, AKT); tumor suppressor → cancer when it LOSES activity (p53, APC). Oncogene = the already-mutated form. (S16, transcript)
Exact mutation verbs: Ras cannot HYDROLYZE GTP (still binds it); AKT always on; p53 cannot be activated/phosphorylated; APC cannot BIND Axin/GSK3 → not a kinase. (S18–S24, transcript)
↑ Bcl-2/↓ Bax → tissue grows; ↑ Bax/↓ Bcl-2 → tissue regresses — not always pathological. Neoplasia/degeneration are the pathological names. (S7, S11, transcript)

quiz.stem: A cell undergoes death in which its DNA is catalytically fragmented, the cytoplasm forms blebs, and no inflammation follows. Which process is this?
quiz.why: Fragmented DNA, blebbing, and no spilled contents (no inflammation) define apoptosis.

quiz.stem: Which example does the lecture give for the REGULATION role of normal apoptosis?
quiz.ok: Removal of excessive CD8+ T cells
bad: Removal of damaged or diseased cells
quiz.why: Regulation = excess CD8+ T cells; maintenance = old liver cells; surveillance = damaged cells; development = digits, neuron pruning.

quiz.stem: Which feature belongs to necrosis and NOT to apoptosis? (ECM = extracellular matrix)
quiz.ok: Cell contents spill into the ECM
bad: Cell is neatly packaged for removal
Cell death proceeds in a controlled way
quiz.why: Necrosis: uncontrolled, acute stress, rupture, contents spilled into ECM, inflammatory.

quiz.stem: A dog has progressive neuron loss in which apoptosis outweighs mitosis. How does the lecture classify this tissue state?
quiz.why: Apoptosis > mitosis = degeneration (e.g. Parkinson's); mitosis > apoptosis = neoplasia.

quiz.stem: Which caspases are the EFFECTOR caspases in this lecture?
quiz.why: Initiators = 8 or 9; effectors = 3, 6, 7.

quiz.stem: After Bax opens mitochondrial membrane pores, what happens NEXT?
quiz.ok: Cytochrome C is released from mitochondria
bad: Bcl-2 transcription rises through p53 activation
FADD is recruited to the trimerized Fas
quiz.why: Bax pores → cytochrome C release → combines with Apaf-1 → apoptosome → procaspase 9.

quiz.stem: Which complex activates procaspase 9 in the internal pathway?
quiz.ok: Apoptosome of cytochrome C and Apaf-1
bad: Death complex of Fas, FasL, and FADD
Pore complex of Bax and mitochondria
Survival complex of Bcl-2 and trophic factors
quiz.why: Cytochrome C + Apaf-1 = apoptosome, which activates procaspase 9.

quiz.stem: A neuron is withdrawn from its trophic (survival) factors. Which outcome is expected from the slides?
bad: Fas trimerizes and recruits FADD protein
Necrosis follows with spilled ECM contents
quiz.why: Trophic factors drive Bcl-2; their removal is listed as a Bax pathway trigger.

quiz.stem: Per the S9 figure, which of the following can trigger the internal (Bax/mitochondrial) apoptosis pathway? (select all that apply)
bad: FasL binding to the Fas receptor
Increased Bcl-2 transcription by trophic factors
quiz.why: S9 lists damage sensing (DNA damage → p53 → Bax) and removal of trophic factors; the figure also shows oxidative stress + calcium (Ca2+) overload acting on mitochondria. FasL is the external pathway; Bcl-2 inhibits.

quiz.stem: In the external pathway, after Fas ligand (FasL) binds the Fas receptor and Fas trimerizes, what is recruited?
bad: Apaf-1 bound to released cytochrome C
quiz.why: FasL binds Fas → trimerizes → recruits FADD → procaspase 8 activated.

quiz.stem: A tumor evades cytotoxic cluster of differentiation 8 (CD8+) T cells by killing them on contact. Based on the Fas ligand (FasL) slide, what does the tumor express?
bad: Fas that binds the T-cell FasL
quiz.why: Tumor anti-immunity: tumor cell expresses FasL, activating Fas/FADD on the T cell → T-cell apoptosis.

quiz.stem: A Ras mutation leaves the protein active WITHOUT a growth signal. What can the mutated Ras no longer do? (GTP = guanosine triphosphate; GDP = guanosine diphosphate)
quiz.why: Mutated Ras cannot hydrolyze GTP, so its off switch fails; it keeps signaling through MAPK.

quiz.stem: Mutated AKT promotes tumorigenesis mainly by which mechanism?
bad: Overproducing Bax to open mitochondrial pores
Freeing E2F by binding Rb protein
quiz.why: Constantly active AKT → high Bcl-2 → internal apoptosis inhibited → overpopulation.

quiz.stem: How does the lecture classify Ras, AKT, p53, and APC?
quiz.ok: Ras, AKT protooncogenes; p53, APC suppressors
bad: Ras, p53 protooncogenes; AKT, APC tumor suppressors
AKT, APC protooncogenes; Ras, p53 suppressors
Ras, APC protooncogenes; AKT, p53 suppressors
quiz.why: Ras and AKT cause cancer when they GAIN activity (proto-oncogenes); p53 and APC when they LOSE activity (tumor suppressors).

quiz.stem: A cell carries p53 that cannot be phosphorylated. After ATM (the damage-sensing kinase) senses DNA damage, what follows? (CDK = cyclin-dependent kinase)
quiz.ok: No p21, so CDK drives the cycle
bad: More p21, so CDK is inhibited
No E2F, so DNA replication stops
quiz.why: Mutated p53 can't respond to ATM → no p21 → no CDK inhibition → cell advances despite damage.

quiz.stem: Mutated APC (a tumor-suppressor gene) cannot bind Axin/GSK3. Which product is constantly transcribed as a result?
quiz.why: No APC–Axin/GSK3 binding → beta-catenin not ubiquitinated → high beta-catenin → cyclin D.

quiz.stem: A 9-year-old German Shepherd has nodular colon masses and neoplastic biopsy cells. Which mutation order fits the colon carcinoma slide?
quiz.why: Normal epithelium → APC → Ras (adenoma) → p53 (carcinoma) → further mutations → metastasis. Slides only: Basel used the case as the intro and did not walk through S32.
quiz.cite: S31, S32 (slides only — likely low priority, confirm)

quiz.stem: Apoptotic cells die without triggering inflammation. Per Dr. Basel, what is the main reason?
quiz.ok: Cytoplasm is packaged in membrane-wrapped blebs
bad: Cytoplasm is released as damage-associated patterns
Caspases digest the immune cells that arrive nearby
Cytochrome C stays sealed inside the mitochondria
quiz.why: Contents stay wrapped in membrane, so nothing spills into the ECM and no damage signals reach immune cells; necrosis ruptures and releases DAMPs.

quiz.stem: A growing tissue receives strong growth factor signaling. Which change pushes its cells away from apoptosis?
quiz.why: Growth factors ↑ Bcl-2, which closes pores; "Bax is bad" and opens pores. p53 (DNA damage) ↑ Bax.

quiz.stem: Cytochrome C has escaped from the mitochondria into the cytoplasm. Which event follows?
quiz.ok: It binds Apaf-1, forming the apoptosome that activates caspase 9
bad: It binds FADD, forming the death complex that activates caspase 8
It binds Bcl-2, forming the pore complex that activates caspase 3
It binds Fas, forming the trimer complex that activates caspase 9
quiz.why: Cytochrome C + Apaf-1 = apoptosome → procaspase 9 → caspase 9 → caspases 3, 6, 7 (internal pathway).

quiz.stem: After FasL binds Fas and FADD activates the first caspase 8, why does caspase 8 rise exponentially?
quiz.ok: Caspase 8 cleaves more procaspase 8 in a loop
bad: Caspase 9 cleaves more procaspase 8 in a loop
Caspase 3 cleaves more procaspase 8 in a loop
Apoptosome cleaves more procaspase 8 in a loop
quiz.why: Basel: caspase 8 cleaves more procaspase 8, so we get an exponential increase before activating caspases 3, 6, 7.

quiz.stem: A newly described gene causes cancer only when a mutation destroys its normal activity. How should it be classified?
quiz.why: Loss of activity → cancer = tumor suppressor (p53, APC). Gain of activity → cancer = proto-oncogene (Ras, AKT).

quiz.stem: During an infection, newly activated CD8+ T cells expand rapidly without killing each other. Why?
quiz.ok: Newly activated T cells do not yet express Fas
bad: Newly activated T cells do not yet express Bax
Newly activated T cells already overexpress Bcl-2
Newly activated T cells do not yet express FADD
quiz.why: New CD8+ cells lack Fas, so no death signal; as they mature they express Fas and kill each other → contraction.
